meaning: The time from the capture of a camera frame to the moment the action computed from it reaches the servos, split into the links that add up to it.
The length of one tick of the host control loop; 33.3 ms at 30 Hz, and the unit a policy's latency is counted in.
One complete run of the policy model, from prepared observation to a decoded chunk of actions.
NVIDIA's family of small computers built to ride on a robot, with an Arm CPU and a GPU sharing one pool of memory.
NVIDIA's desk-side Arm computer with a GPU and 128 GB of memory shared between CPU and GPU.
NVIDIA's software bundle for Jetson devices: Linux, GPU drivers and libraries.
One pool of physical memory addressed by both the CPU and the GPU, so the GPU does not get the whole of it.
Playing a chunk to its end, then calling the model and waiting, which pauses the arm between chunks.
Starting the next policy call early, while the current chunk is still playing.
Real-time chunking: computes the next action chunk while the current one plays and, by inpainting, makes it continue the motion already committed.
LeRobot's arrangement in which a policy server holds the checkpoint and the robot computer keeps the cameras, motors and recording.
A publish/subscribe network protocol; LeRobot uses it to carry observations to the policy server and chunks back.
LeRobot's setting for how much playback may remain in the queue when the client asks for the next chunk.
The measured round trip of one remote policy request, from encoding through network and inference to decoding.
NVIDIA's inference compiler and runtime, which turns a model graph into an engine tuned for one kind of GPU.
The file TensorRT writes: a model compiled for the GPU type and TensorRT version it was built with, which fails to deserialize elsewhere.
A portable file format for a model graph, used as the hand-off between a trained checkpoint and the device.
A major.minor number naming a GPU generation, recorded in an engine and checked when it loads.
A TensorRT build option that makes an engine loadable on other GPU types; in 11.5.0 it exists on Arm server-class Linux and not on JetPack.
Storing a model's numbers in fewer bits so each layer moves less memory and does cheaper arithmetic.
A sixteen-bit floating-point format that keeps FP32's eight-bit exponent and gives up mantissa bits; the unquantised default for GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5.
NVIDIA's 4-bit floating-point format with per-block scaling, supported natively by the GPU in Jetson Thor.
A suite of simulated manipulation tasks used as a benchmark for robot policies.
Devices outside the data centre that connect to a cloud service; here, the robot computer.
An AWS edge runtime and cloud service: a program on the device runs the software the cloud service tells it to.
The Greengrass program installed on the device, which installs, starts and watches components.
The smaller Greengrass nucleus written in C, with a shorter feature list than the Java nucleus.
The unit of software Greengrass runs: a recipe plus its artifacts.
A JSON or YAML file that defines a component's details, dependencies, artifacts and lifecycle commands.
A file a component needs on the device, such as a script, a binary or a container image.
The part of a recipe that holds the commands to install, start and stop a component.
The AWS-provided Greengrass component that pulls container images, including from private Amazon ECR repositories.
AWS's store for container images.
A local Greengrass server that trades the device certificate for temporary AWS credentials, so no access key sits on the device.
The identity file issued to a device when it is registered, which it uses to prove who it is to AWS IoT.
The AWS service that defines roles and what each role may call.
NVIDIA's robot policy, whose deployment README gives median call times on Jetson Orin, Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark.
Physical Intelligence's vision-language-action model with a flow-matching action head, used in the real-time chunking papers and NVIDIA's Thor tutorial.
A policy that reads camera images and a text instruction and outputs robot actions.
A run of future actions returned by one policy call and played one per control tick.
The middle value of a set of timed calls: the typical call, not the slowest.
Our arithmetic from LeRobot's tuning rule: an asynchronous call must take at most half of what its chunk lasts, L <= H dt / 2.
In the real-time chunking paper, d = floor(delta / dt): a call's length counted in whole control periods.
The image-editing task of filling a missing region so it matches its surroundings; real-time chunking treats the start of a new chunk the same way.
The three parts of a new chunk under real-time chunking: actions already played from the old chunk, actions pulled toward the old chunk with a decaying weight, and new actions past its end.
LeRobot's RTC argument for the call's latency in control steps, passed with every call because it varies at run time.
LeRobot's RTC setting for how many actions of the old chunk the new one stays consistent with; 10 by default, typically 8 to 12.
LeRobot's RTC cap on how hard the new chunk is pulled toward the old one; 10.0 by default.
LeRobot's RTC setting for the shape of the decaying guidance weight; the code defaults to LINEAR, the documentation recommends EXP.
LeRobot's default RTC mode: guidance at run time, working with ordinary flow-matching checkpoints.
LeRobot's RTC mode for checkpoints trained with training-time RTC: the prefix is fed in, with no guidance at run time.
A later method that trains the model with a random delay and a clean prefix, so no guidance or backward pass is needed at run time.
The gradient computation of training; guided RTC runs one at every denoising step.
One pass of a flow-matching action head, which builds a chunk from noise in a few such passes.
Averaging overlapping chunks with weights; on real robots with added delay it oscillated into protective stops.
The robot's built-in safety halt.
LeRobot remote inference's default: drop incoming actions whose time has passed and replace only the future part of the queue.
LeRobot's per-run timing summary of each stage of the control loop, including infer, observe, send and pacing headroom.
In LeRobot's cadence report, the time left in a tick after the loop's work; near zero leaves nothing to absorb a slow tick.
LeRobot's grace period, 1 s by default, for which a supported robot holds its last target when the action queue runs dry before the run faults.
The full-precision format; GR00T N1.7's vision encoder stays at FP32.
A sixteen-bit format with a five-bit exponent; it overflows in pi0.5's attention layers.
Eight bits with four for the exponent and three for the mantissa, as TensorRT 11.5 documents it.
Four bits with two for the exponent and one for the mantissa; NVFP4 adds a scale per block.
Running real samples through a model to choose the scales for its quantised layers; NVIDIA's recipe uses 10 samples of robot data.
How closely two output vectors point the same way; 1.0 is the same direction.
Splitting one GPU into isolated instances, each with its own compute, cache and memory bandwidth.
The bits of a floating-point number that set how large or small it can get.
The bits of a floating-point number that set how finely it is stored.
In the real-time chunking paper, s: how many actions of a chunk play before the next chunk takes over. LeRobot uses the same name for a different setting, execution_horizon.
Running several of a model's matrix multiplications as one GPU kernel; part of NVIDIA's optimised execution profile for GR00T N1.7 on Thor.
A sequence of GPU kernel launches recorded once and started again with one call.
